Introduction

Microvellum stores its libraries and company data in a SQL Server database. Before Microvellum can be installed for a shop or connected across a network, something has to host that database — and that "something" is a small, free edition of Microsoft's database engine called SQL Server Express.

This guide combines and re-explains two of Microvellum's official Community tutorials — Installing SQL Server Express Edition and Configuring an SQL Express Database — as one continuous walkthrough, with plain-language explanations added for anyone who hasn't set up SQL Server before. If you can follow a wizard and copy-paste a password into a text file, you can do this.

What you'll end up with A working named SQL Server Express instance, reachable over the network, with one database created and one login mapped to it — ready for Microvellum to connect to.

Before you start

Set aside about 45–60 minutes, most of which is unattended install time. Work through these before touching the installer:

  • Back up any existing company data configurations and library data
  • Fully close AutoCAD and every Microvellum product on the machine
  • Confirm you have local administrator rights on this computer
  • Know whether this machine is a domain controller (if so, install elsewhere — see note below)
  • Have a password manager or secure note ready for the sa password
Don't install on a domain controller Microsoft does not support running SQL Server on the same machine that acts as your network's domain controller. Pick any other Windows machine or server on the network.

Part 1Installing SQL Server Express

This part installs the database engine itself and creates a named instance — the "container" that will eventually hold Microvellum's database. Later, in Part 2, you'll open that instance up to the network and put data in it.

1

Download & unblock the installer

Grab the installer from Microsoft directly — not from a mirror or forum link:

  1. Download SQL Server 2022 Express and save it somewhere you can find it again.
  2. Right-click the downloaded file → Properties → tick Unblock (if present) → OK. Windows flags files downloaded from the internet; unblocking tells it you trust this one.
  3. Right-click the file again → Run as administrator, then click Yes on the User Account Control prompt.
2

Launch the Installation Center

The installer unpacks itself, asks where to place its files (the default location is fine unless you have a reason to change it), and then opens the SQL Server Installation Center. Choose the standalone install option:

Skip SSRS You only need SQL Server Reporting Services if you plan to build reports outside Microvellum. Most shops can ignore that link entirely.
3

Accept the license & choose your update settings

Read the Microsoft License Terms, check the acceptance box, and click Next. On the update settings screen, Microvellum recommends leaving automatic updates off — an unplanned SQL Server update is a common, avoidable cause of "it worked yesterday" support calls.

4

Let the Install Rules check run

Setup automatically checks a handful of system requirements before it lets you continue.

A Windows Firewall warning is expected and fine to click past, as long as you plan to open the ports it's warning you about:

Ports to allowTCP 1433 & UDP 1434

Your network and firewall should already be configured before you get here — doing it after the fact just means an extra reboot or service restart. See general firewall guidance or the Database Engine–specific instructions from Microsoft.

5

Feature Selection

The defaults are correct for a Microvellum database server — you don't need to hand-pick features here.

6

Instance Configuration — name your instance

An instance is simply a self-contained copy of the database engine running on this machine — you can have more than one, each with its own name. If you don't already have a naming convention, the default SQLEXPRESS is fine.

7

Server Configuration — SQL Server Browser

Switch the SQL Server Browser service's Startup Type to Automatic if it isn't already. This is the service that lets other computers on the network find your named instance by name instead of by a specific port.

8

Database Engine Configuration — authentication & the sa account

This is the step most worth slowing down for. Choose Mixed Mode so that both Windows accounts and SQL Server's own logins can connect — Microvellum environments typically need this. Then set a strong password for sa, the built-in System Administrator account, and store it somewhere safe.

Don't lose this password There's no "forgot password" link for the sa account. If you lose it and no Windows administrator account was added here, you'll need to reinstall to regain access.
9

Let it install

Setup now applies everything you've configured. Depending on the machine, this can take up to 30 minutes — a good point to grab coffee. When it finishes, SQL Server 2022 Express is installed, but it's still only reachable from the local machine. Part 2 opens it up to the network and gives it a database.

Part 2Configuring the SQL Express Database

Picking up where Part 1 left off: your instance exists but can't yet talk to other computers, and it has no databases in it. This part fixes both.

1

Turn on TCP/IP networking

Open SQL Server 2022 Configuration Manager (press the Windows key and search for it, or find it under Start → Microsoft SQL Server 2022), approve the User Account Control prompt, then:

  1. Expand SQL Server Network Configuration
  2. Select Protocols for <your instance name>
  3. Double-click TCP/IP, set Enabled to Yes, then Apply → OK
Why this matters By default, a fresh SQL Server Express install only accepts connections from the same machine (via Shared Memory). Enabling TCP/IP is what lets other computers on the network — including the machines running Microvellum — reach this instance at all.
2

Restart the SQL Server service

Network protocol changes don't take effect until the service restarts. In the same Configuration Manager window, expand SQL Server Services, right-click your instance, and choose Restart. Then close Configuration Manager.

3

Install SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)

SSMS is the free graphical tool you'll use to actually manage the database — SQL Server Express itself has no user interface of its own. Download the current version of SSMS from Microsoft, right-click the installer → Run as administrator, approve the User Account Control prompt, click Install, then Close once it finishes.

4

Connect for the first time

Open SSMS from the Start menu. In the Connect to Server dialog, the Server name field should already show <Computer Name>\<Instance Name> — for example DESKTOP-U3Q120A\SQLEXPRESS. Change the Authentication dropdown to SQL Server Authentication and sign in with the sa account and the password you set back in Part 1.

5

Create the database

In SSMS's Object Explorer, right-click Databases → New Database. Give it a name that will still make sense in a year — something reflecting the company or library version, not just "test."

6

Create a login for whoever needs access

Expand Security → Logins, right-click, and choose New Login. You have two options, covered in more detail in the comparison table below:

  • Windows Authentication (recommended on a domain) — click Search…, then Locations… → Entire Directory, type the username, and click Check Names to confirm it resolves before clicking OK.
  • SQL Server Authentication (for peer-to-peer / non-domain networks) — enter a login name and password directly; you may need to relax the password-complexity requirement depending on your policy.
7

Map the login to the database

Still in the new login's properties, open the User Mapping page, tick the checkbox next to the database you created, then — in the role list below — tick db_owner so this login can actually read and write data, not just connect.

You're done At this point you have a reachable SQL Server Express instance, a named database, and a login that owns it. Point Microvellum's database configuration at this server/instance name and this login, and you're ready to go.

Windows vs. SQL Server authentication, at a glance

You'll be asked to pick one of these twice in this guide — once for the server's overall authentication mode, once per login you create. Here's the difference in plain terms:

 Windows AuthenticationSQL Server Authentication
How you sign inUses your existing Windows/domain account — no separate passwordA separate username and password stored inside SQL Server
Best forOffices on a Windows domain / Active DirectoryPeer-to-peer networks, workgroups, or machines with no domain
Managed byYour network administrator, centrallyWhoever manages the SQL Server instance directly
Typical accountDOMAIN\usernamesa or a custom SQL login

Choosing Mixed Mode during install (Part 1, step 8) simply means the server will accept either kind of login — it doesn't commit you to one or the other for every account you create afterward.

Glossary

Authentication Mode
The server-wide setting that decides whether SQL Server accepts Windows logins only, or both Windows and SQL Server logins (Mixed Mode).
Database Engine
The core SQL Server component that actually stores and retrieves data — as opposed to reporting, analysis, or management tools that sit on top of it.
db_owner
A built-in database role that grants full read/write/administer rights over one specific database, without granting rights over the whole server.
Instance (named instance)
A self-contained, independently-running copy of SQL Server on one machine, identified by a name such as SQLEXPRESS. A single machine can host several instances side by side.
Instance ID
The short identifier baked into an instance's file paths on disk. Usually matches the instance name unless you deliberately change it during setup.
License Terms
Microsoft's end-user license agreement (EULA) for SQL Server, which you must accept before setup will proceed.
Login vs. User
A login grants access to the SQL Server instance as a whole; a user is that same identity's presence inside one specific database. User Mapping is what connects the two.
Mixed Mode
An authentication mode that accepts both Windows Authentication and SQL Server Authentication logins on the same instance.
Named Pipes / Shared Memory
Older, local-only connection protocols SQL Server can use. Shared Memory is fastest but only works for connections originating on the same machine — which is why TCP/IP must be enabled for network access.
Peer-to-peer network
A small network with no central domain controller, where each computer manages its own accounts. Common in small shops; favors SQL Server Authentication over Windows Authentication.
SSRS Reporting Services
An optional add-on for building and distributing reports. Not required unless you need reports outside of Microvellum itself.
sa account
The built-in "System Administrator" SQL Server login, created automatically in Mixed Mode. Has unrestricted rights — treat its password like a master key.
SQL Server Authentication
A login method where SQL Server itself stores a username and password, independent of Windows accounts.
SQL Server Browser
A Windows service that lets client computers find a named SQL Server instance by name over the network, rather than needing to know its exact port number.
SQL Server Configuration Manager
The utility used to enable/disable network protocols (like TCP/IP) and to start, stop, or restart SQL Server's Windows services.
SSDT Data Tools
A Visual Studio–based toolset for database development projects. Not needed for a standard Microvellum installation.
SQL Server Express
The free, feature-limited edition of Microsoft SQL Server, suitable for smaller databases such as those Microvellum uses.
SSMS Management Studio
The free graphical application used to connect to, browse, and manage SQL Server databases, logins, and permissions.
TCP/IP (protocol)
The network protocol that must be enabled in Configuration Manager before any other computer can connect to a SQL Server instance.
User Account Control (UAC)
The Windows "Do you want to allow this app to make changes?" prompt. SQL Server setup and configuration tools require administrator rights, so expect to see it often.
User Mapping
The step that links a server-level login to a specific database and assigns it a role (such as db_owner) inside that database.
Windows Authentication
A login method that trusts the user's existing Windows or domain account instead of a separate SQL Server password.
Windows Firewall exception (ports 1433 / 1434)
A firewall rule that must allow TCP port 1433 (the database engine) and UDP port 1434 (SQL Server Browser) for network clients to reach the instance.
